newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers, employers talk through night.
newsitem.headline: French truckers, employers talk through night.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers and their employers searched for an end to their impasse in marathon talks on Tuesday as trucker roadblocks kept freight shipments at a standstill and threatened to dry up petrol supplies.
As the trucker protest entered its ninth day, union officials said it was growing in strength and putting greater pressure on the economy in the most serious labour unrest in France this year.

Roger Poletti, spokesman for the Workers Force (FO) trade union, said that the number of roadblocks had risen to 180 by Monday evening from 136 earlier in the day, with tens of thousands of trucks blockading motorways, borders and fuel depots.

FO leader Marc Blondel met Transport Minister Bernard Pons and threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal was reached by Tuesday on truckers' demands for higher wages, shorter hours and retirement at 55 rather than 60.

"What I can say very clearly is that if there is not a result by tomorrow (Tuesday) morning, Workers Force will examine the conditions for extending the movement to transport," Blondel told reporters.
Nicole Notat, leader of the French Workers Confederation (CFDT), issued what she called "a final appeal for reason on the part of employers".
"This is what the truckers are impatiently waiting for. They are not carrying out this struggle for the pleasure of inconveniencing people," she told France 2 television.

The Communist-led CGT called on its members to widen their protests with a national day of demonstrations and rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday, and five rail unions urged their members to support the strikes "with the appropriate means".
Truckers blocked Channel ports and German border crossings and tightened their noose on oil refineries and fuel depots after earlier all-night talks ended in deadlock on Monday.
Officials in some parts of the country were taking steps to limit petrol sales and prevent motorists from hoarding ever scarcer supplies.
Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe renewed his appeal for a deal to end the strike that was putting a stranglehold on the economy and provoking friction with France's neighbours.

"I'm following the talks hour by hour," he said before the latest round of talks chaired by government mediator Robert Cros. "The government has done everything to get these talks under way. They must now resume and finish."

A German truck driver became the first serious casualty of the strike on Monday when French truckers pelted his lorry with stones at a roadblock near Chalon-sur-Saone in eastern France. The driver from the Stuttgart region, whose name was witheld, suffered head wounds and underwent emergency surgery in Dijon.
The unrest showed signs of spreading to other sectors.

Trade unions announced plans for a 24-hour strike at state-owned utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France on December 3, and for a two-day strike at Air France and other French airlines on Wednesday and Thursday.
"It is time for all air transport staff to mobilise against provocation by the public authorities and the management of Air France," a CFDT statement said.
The trucker dispute was the most serious unrest since a 24-day round of public sector strikes against the centre-right government almost paralysed the country late last year.
